In the US, stocks are listed on one exchange but can be traded on multiple venues.  You need to confirm exactly what your data is showing: a) trades on the primary-listed exchange; or b) trades made at any venue. Also, the trade condition codes are important.  Only certain trade condition codes contribute towards the day's open/high/low/close and some others only contribute towards the volume data.  The Consolidated Tape Association is very clear on which trades should contribute towards each value - but some vendors have their own interpretation (or just simply an erroneous interpretation of the specifications). It may surprise you to find that the majority of trading volume for many stocks is not on their primary-listed exchange.  For example, on 2 Mar 2015, NASDAQ:AAPL traded a total volume across all venues was 48096663 shares but trading on NASDAQ itself was 12050277 shares. Trades can be cancelled.  Some data vendors do not modify their data to reflect these busted trades.   Some data vendors also  snapshot  their feed at a particular point in time of the data.  Some exchanges can provide data (mainly corrections) 4-5 hours after the closing bell.  By snapshotting the data too early and throwing away any subsequent data is a typical cause of data discrepancies.   Some data vendors also round prices/volumes - but stocks don't just trade to two decimal places. So you may well be comparing two different sets of trades (with their own specific inclusion rules) against the same stock.  You need to confirm with your data sources exactly how they do things. Disclosure: Premium Data is an end-of-day daily data vendor.

A lease is a rental plain and simple.  You borrow money to finance the expected depreciation over the course of the lease term.  This arrangement will almost always cost more over time of your  ownership.   That does not mean that a lease is always a worse  deal.    Cars are almost always a losing proposition; save for the oddball Porsche or Ferrari that is too scarce relative to demand.  You accept ownership of a car and it starts to lose value.  New cars lose value faster than used cars.  Typically, if you were to purchase the car, then sell it after 3 years, the total cost over those three years will work out to less total money than the equivalent 36 month lease.  But, you will have to come up with a lot more money down, or a higher monthly payment, and/or sell the car after 36 months (assuming the pretty standard 36 month lease).  With this in mind, some cars lease better than others because the projected depreciation is more favorable than other brands or models.   Personally, I bought a slightly used car certified pre-owned with a agreeable factory warranty extension.  My next car I may lease.  Late model cars are getting so unbelievably expensive to maintain that more and more I feel like a long term rental has merit. Just understand that for the convenience, for the freeing up of your cash flow, for the unlikelihood of maintenance, to not bother with resale or trading the car in, a lease will cost a premium over a purchase over the same time frame.

In statistics, classification is the problem of identifying which of a set of categories (sub-populations) an observation (or observations) belongs to.  Examples are assigning a given email to the  spam  or  non-spam  class, and assigning a diagnosis to a given patient based on observed characteristics of the patient (sex, blood pressure, presence or absence of certain symptoms, etc.).
Often, the individual observations are analyzed into a set of quantifiable properties, known variously as explanatory variables or features.  These properties may variously be categorical (e.g.  A ,  B ,  AB  or  O , for blood type), ordinal (e.g.  large ,  medium  or  small ), integer-valued (e.g. the number of occurrences of a particular word in an email) or real-valued (e.g. a measurement of blood pressure). Other classifiers work by comparing observations to previous observations by means of a similarity or distance function.
An algorithm that implements classification, especially in a concrete implementation, is known as a classifier.  The term  classifier  sometimes also refers to the mathematical function, implemented by a classification algorithm, that maps input data to a category.
Terminology across fields is quite varied. In statistics, where classification is often done with logistic regression or a similar procedure, the properties of observations are termed explanatory variables (or independent variables, regressors, etc.), and the categories to be predicted are known as outcomes, which are considered to be possible values of the dependent variable.  In machine learning, the observations are often known as instances, the explanatory variables are termed features (grouped into a feature vector), and the possible categories to be predicted are classes.  Other fields may use different terminology: e.g. in community ecology, the term  classification  normally refers to cluster analysis.

Digital signatures rely on something called public key cryptography . You 're probably familiar with a [ rotation cipher ] ( URL_0 ) . This is where you encode a message by substituting one letter for another letter that is later in the alphabet . The number of letters you shift over is called the * key * . If your key is 1 , then encrypting a message works like this : A = > B , B = > C , C = > D , etc . If your key is 5 , encrypting works like this : A = > F , B = > G , C = > H , etc . You send this message to a friend , who knows the key you used . They take each letter , count backwards in the alphabet the amount that the key says , and substitute letters that way . If they do it right , they should get the original message back . This is an example of _ symmetric key cryptography _ , because the same key ( the number 5 ) was used to both encrypt and decrypt the message . Symmetric key cryptography is awesome and useful , but it ca n't be used to create digital signatures . Enter public key cryptography . In public key cryptography , there are two keys . We 'll call them A and B for now . The way this works is that any message encrypted using key A can only be decrypted with key B. Also , any message encrypted with key B can only be decrypted with key A. Also , if you only have one of the keys , it 's impossible to figure out what the other key is . There are a couple different ways to do this , but the most common is called RSA . There are lots of articles and videos about RSA if you want to learn more about it . Now that you have your two keys , A and B , you pick one of them ( let 's say A ) , and publish it somewhere where everyone can see it . This is your * public key * . You keep the other one ( B ) secret . Now , if someone wants to send you a message , they can encrypt the message with key A. Since you 're the only person with key B , only you will be able to read it . But , remember , you can do things the other way around . If you encrypt something with key B , anyone with key A can decrypt it and read it . But since key A is public , and everyone has key A , that means anyone can decrypt your message , so what good is it ? Well , key A only works with messages encrypted with key B. Since you 're the only person with key B , then by decrypting this message , the whole world can be sure that * you * sent the message . The fact that the message can be decrypted with your public key is like having your unique signature on the message . This is the basic idea behind digital signatures . So , let 's say I want to send you a secret message , and when you receive it , you want to be sure it was me that sent it . We each generate a public and private key . We tell each other our public keys . I take the secret message and first encrypt it with my private key . I have effectively signed the message , but anyone with my public key can still read it . So , I encrypt it with your public key . I send it to you , you decrypt it with your private key , then decrypt it again with my public key . You now have a secret message that only I could have sent .

A paradox is an impossible situation . More specifically a paradox is a seemingly reasonable statement that leads to an impossible conclusion . Often times this conclusion is a lack thereof due to a circular logic . The most simple one is the statement   This statement is false   . If the statement is false , then it is true . If it is true , then it is false . Imagine a man goes back in time and kills his grandfather before the grandfather meets his grandmother . By killing his grandfather , the man causes his father to not be born which means the men is not born and can not go back in time to kill his grandfather . If he ca n't go back in time to kill his grandfather , then his grandfather lives and the man eventually is born and goes back in time to kill his grandfather . This is a classic example known as   The Grandfather Paradox   Several deal with the idea of an omnipotent , omniscient , morally perfect God . * Free Will- if God is all knowing and knows what we will decide , then we are n't actually deciding anything because it is already known and therefore predetermined . * Can God create a stone so heavy he can not lift it ? If he ca n't create a stone he ca n't lift , then it shows he is limited in what he can do . If he can not lift the stone , then it also shows he has limitations . * If God is all - knowing , all - powerful , and morally perfect , then why does he allow suffering in the world ? The article actually explained it pretty well . Basically , you tell someone you will buy their widget now for $ 1 , but you will give an identical widget back to them in a month . So it 's kinda like renting the widget , except you fully own the widget and can do whatever you want to it during the month you own it . Smash it , burn it , whatever . As long as you give an identical widget back to the person at the end of the month , they do n't care . Now you sell the widget . Currently , widgets cost $ 10 . So you gain $ 10 . But you still owe the person a widget . Now , suppose the price of widgets drops . At the end of the month , the day before you have to give the widget back , widgets only cost $ 6 . You spend $ 6 and buy the widget . You give the widget back to the person . You spent $ 1 ( widget rental ) and $ 6 ( buy a new widget ) , but you gained $ 10 ( widget sale ) . So on the balance , you are $ 3 richer . But only because the cost of widgets went down . Suppose the cost of widgets went from $ 10 to $ 12 . You had to spend $ 1 ( widget rental feel ) and $ 12 ( buy a new widget ) , but only made $ 10 . You now have $ 3 less than when you started ! This is why short - selling is dangerous . You have to be absolutely sure the price of widgets will go down , and you have to know exactly when . If you get either of these things wrong , you lose money . Maybe a lot of money , if you bought a lot of widgets or if widgets are very expensive .

Wood is not a single thing , it 's a bunch of stuff arranged together to make what we call wood . There 's water , carbon , and a whole bunch of other stuff in it . Each of these has its own temperature that it becomes liquid and gas , as well as the temperature it burns at . For some things , the   burn   temperature is lower than the temperature it melts at , or lower than the temperature of the other stuff in the wood . When wood is heated the stuff in it starts to break down from the heat . The water changes from liquid to gas and other stuff starts to change because of both the heat and the water boiling away . Then some of the stuff in the wood begins to burn because it is higher than its   combustion point   ( a fancy way of saying how hot it can get before it burns ) . The heat released by the stuff beginning to burn raises the temperature even further and other stuff begins to burn . The biggest reason that wood does n't melt is really that the stuff that 's in it will mostly burn before it melts .

Suppose there 's two persons : Mary Baker and John Farmer . Mary 's a baker , John 's a wheat farmer . Therefore , Mary often buys wheat , John often sells it . Now , John has two problems : 1 . How does he plan how much wheat to grow during the season ? If he grows too much , he will have spent too much money on seed , fertilizer , etc . If he grows too little , he will not have earned as much money as he could have . 2 . Suppose he makes his plan , grows the wheat , but then at when it 's ready , the price of wheat has dropped a lot . In this case , he may lose money — or at least not make the profit he expected . Mary also has a problem . She makes most of her money from wedding cakes . Everybody gets married in the same season , but they want to know the price of the cake six months before the wedding . But Mary does n't know how much wheat will cost when she makes the cakes — so if she gives a quote with current wheat prices , and the price goes up , she may end up losing money . There 's a way to solve all of these problems in one shot : John and Mary come to an agreement where Mary will buy John 's wheat 6 months from now , but at today 's wheat price . This way , John knows how much wheat to grow and how much he will be paid for it , and Mary knows how much she will pay for her wheat as well . Well , futures trading is basically what you get when you recognize that this idea can be improved by making it work like sports betting : * We have a bookie ( the futures exchange ) that takes bets on the price of wheat — always taking a bit off the top as payment . * Mary figures out how much wheat she will need , and then she goes to the bookie and offers a bet that wheat prices will go up . The size of the bet is based on how much wheat she will need , and she wins or loses money proportionate to how far the price ends up from today 's price . So now , if wheat goes up she loses on the cakes but makes up for it by the earnings of the bet . ( If wheat goes down , she loses on her bet but spends less on the wheat for the cakes . ) * John goes to the bookie as well , sees Mary 's offered bet , and accepts the other side of it — he bets that wheat prices will go down . He uses the amount of Mary 's ( and other people 's ) bets to plan how much wheat to grow . That way he does n't grow too much wheat , and if wheat prices actually go down , he makes less on his wheat but wins it back from the bet . So that achieves the same thing as the first solution , but Mary and John did n't even need to know about each other — they just deal with a common third party ( the bookie / futures exchange ) .

This is a really good question . If I understand it right , you 're asking about the reason why the scale sounds good without a black note between e / f or b / c. There 's a nice math - based answer . First , you need to know about   beat frequencies .   In short , if two musical notes have frequencies A and B , then the notes have * low * beat frequency with each other if you can write the fraction A / B using fairly small numbers . Low beat frequency sounds good to humans , and high beat frequency sounds bad . The fancy musical term for low / high beat frequency is   consonance   and   dissonance ,   respectively . Under this rule , what note pair should sound * the best * ? Well , if your first note has frequency F , then you want your second note to have frequency 2*F. Then F/2F = 1/2 , which can be written using small numbers , so it ought to sound good , right ? This is an octave : every time you go up an octave on a piano , you double the note frequency . Aside from octaves , what else should sound good ? If our first note has frequency F , then the next best candidates should be , in order : ( 3/2)F , ( 4/3)F , ( 5/3)F , ( 5/4)F , ( 6/5)F. In a truly wild and beautiful coincidence of the universe , these fractions are approximately equal to : 2^(7/12 ) , 2^(5/12 ) , 2^(9/12 ) , 2^(4/12 ) , and 2^(2/12 ) . * * The   12   in the bottom of those fractions is why music sounds good to humans ! * * So now we know that it 's a good idea to split the octave into 12 equal parts . That 's why there are 12 notes ( including black ones ) in an octave . We also know that we should pay special attention to the 2nd , 4th , 5th , 7th , and 9th of these twelve notes . If the original note was a C , then these new notes are D , E , F , G , A. That answers one of your questions : * * the reason there is no black note between E and F is that , by coincidence , the second and third low - beat - frequency powers of 2^(1/12 ) are only one away from each other . * * B is a bit of a bastard child here . The reason it sounds good is that it has low beat frequency with D , E , and G , which obviously tend to appear a lot in the scale of C. Some classical composers went so far as to declare B a   black note   and not part of the major scale , but I guess now we 've decided that it plays nicely with DEG and that 's good enough for us . So that 's why we allow B = 2^(11/12 ) into the white key club , and so there can be no half - step between B and C. Quick aside : There 's a decent case to be made that we should use B flat = 2^(10/12 ) instead of B = 2^(11/12 ) . People do this , sometimes , and it 's called a   Dorian mode . Computational geometry is a branch of computer science devoted to the study of algorithms which can be stated in terms of geometry. Some purely geometrical problems arise out of the study of computational geometric algorithms, and such problems are also considered to be part of computational geometry. While modern computational geometry is a recent development, it is one of the oldest fields of computing with a history stretching back to antiquity.
Computational complexity is central to computational geometry, with great practical significance if algorithms are used on very large datasets containing tens or hundreds of millions of points. For such sets, the difference between O(n2) and O(n log n) may be the difference between days and seconds of computation.
The main impetus for the development of computational geometry as a discipline was progress in computer graphics and computer-aided design and manufacturing (CAD/CAM), but many problems in computational geometry are classical in nature, and may come from mathematical visualization.
Other important applications of computational geometry include robotics (motion planning and visibility problems), geographic information systems (GIS) (geometrical location and search, route planning), integrated circuit design (IC geometry design and verification), computer-aided engineering (CAE) (mesh generation), and computer vision (3D reconstruction).

Active contour model, also called snakes, is a framework in computer vision introduced by Michael Kass, Andrew Witkin, and Demetri Terzopoulos for delineating an object outline from a possibly noisy 2D image. The snakes model is popular in computer vision, and snakes are widely used in applications like object tracking, shape recognition, segmentation, edge detection and stereo matching.
A snake is an energy minimizing, deformable spline influenced by constraint and image forces that pull it towards object contours and internal forces that resist deformation. Snakes may be understood as a special case of the general technique of matching a deformable model to an image by means of energy minimization. In two dimensions, the active shape model represents a discrete version of this approach, taking advantage of the point distribution model to restrict the shape range to an explicit domain learnt from a training set.
Snakes do not solve the entire problem of finding contours in images, since the method requires knowledge of the desired contour shape beforehand. Rather, they depend on other mechanisms such as interaction with a user, interaction with some higher level image understanding process, or information from image data adjacent in time or space.

The ocean - atmosphere system is extremely complex and there are still many unknowns , so there is no particularly simple answer to this question . But as a generalisation , it would be more correct to say that winds drive oceanic currents than the other way around . Winds have a very important impact on ocean circulation and they are the cause of the large gyres that dominate most ocean basins . The other main driver of ocean circulation is the thermohaline circulation ( driven by density differences ) . The North Atlantic is a good example that illustrates both - the Gulf Stream is largely wind - driven , whereas the large - scale sinking of cold , saline waters around Iceland is thermohaline driven . Ocean circulation does have an impact on winds . The oceans are a significant mode of heat transport on the earth so without them , the winds would be stronger . The resulting changes in heat distribution can also affect wind patterns . But generally speaking , the large - scale patterns in the wind are not really caused by ocean circulation whereas ocean circulation most definitely is controlled to a large extent by wind . Of course , the ultimate driver of both is radiation from the sun .

We're trying to figure out what to do next.  In terms of planning, the sunk cost is irrelevant.  But in terms of calculating return, A was a turkey. Sunk costs are irrelevant to planning, but they are very relevant to retrospective analysis.  Please don't confuse the two.  When looking back, part of the cost for B will be that $X.  But in the middle, after paying $X and before starting B, the $X is gone.  You only have the building and have to make your decision based on the options you have at that moment.   You will sometimes hear $Y called the opportunity cost of B.  You could sell out for $Y or you could do B.  You should only do B if it is worth more than $Y.   The sunk cost fallacy would be comparing B to $X.  Assuming $Y is less than $X, this would make you not do B when it is your best path forward from that moment.  I.e. $Y < NPV(B) < $X means that you should do the project.  You will lose money (apparently that's a foregone conclusion), but you will lose less money than if you just sold out.   You should also do B if $Y < $X < NPV(B) or $X < $Y < NPV(B).  In general, you should do B any time $Y < NPV(B).  The only time you should not do B is if NPV(B) < $Y. So if you had a positive charge it would move from high potential to low potential , and if you had a negative charge it would move from low potential to high potential . They essentially found a way to figure out , in space , which areas were the peaks , and which areas were the valleys , and positive electrical charge rolls down from the peaks of potential to the valleys of potential . Soar is a cognitive architecture, originally created by John Laird, Allen Newell, and Paul Rosenbloom at Carnegie Mellon University. (Rosenbloom continued to serve as co-principal investigator after moving to Stanford University, then to the University of Southern California's Information Sciences Institute.) It is now maintained and developed by John Laird's research group at the University of Michigan.
The goal of the Soar project is to develop the fixed computational building blocks necessary for general intelligent agents – agents that can perform a wide range of tasks and encode, use, and learn all types of knowledge to realize the full range of cognitive capabilities found in humans, such as decision making, problem solving, planning, and natural-language understanding. It is both a theory of what cognition is and a computational implementation of that theory. Since its beginnings in 1983 as John Laird’s thesis, it has been widely used by AI researchers to create intelligent agents and cognitive models of different aspects of human behavior. The most current and comprehensive description of Soar is the 2012 book, The Soar Cognitive Architecture.

As you probably know, a credit spread involves buying a call (or put) at one strike and selling another call (or put) at another with the same maturity, so you're dealing with two orders. They also don't care what the individual prices are; they just care what the difference is. The exchange never sees your actual limit order; they will just see the market orders placed by your broker.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is a medical imaging technique used in radiology to form pictures of the anatomy and the physiological processes of the body. MRI scanners use strong magnetic fields, magnetic field gradients, and radio waves to generate images of the organs in the body. MRI does not involve X-rays or the use of ionizing radiation, which distinguishes it from CT and PET scans. MRI is a medical application of nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) which can also be used for imaging in other NMR applications, such as NMR spectroscopy.
MRI is widely used in hospitals and clinics for medical diagnosis, staging and follow-up of disease. Compared to CT, MRI provides better contrast in images of soft-tissues, e.g. in the brain or abdomen. However, it may be perceived as less comfortable by patients, due to the usually longer and louder measurements with the subject in a long, confining tube, though  Open  MRI designs mostly relieve this. Additionally, implants and other non-removable metal in the body can pose a risk and may exclude some patients from undergoing an MRI examination safely.
MRI was originally called NMRI (nuclear magnetic resonance imaging), but  nuclear  was dropped to avoid negative associations. Certain atomic nuclei are able to absorb radio frequency energy when placed in an external magnetic field; the resultant evolving spin polarization can induce a RF signal in a radio frequency coil and thereby be detected. In clinical and research MRI, hydrogen atoms are most often used to generate a macroscopic polarization that is detected by antennas close to the subject being examined. Hydrogen atoms are naturally abundant in humans and other biological organisms, particularly in water and fat. For this reason, most MRI scans essentially map the location of water and fat in the body. Pulses of radio waves excite the nuclear spin energy transition, and magnetic field gradients localize the polarization in space. By varying the parameters of the pulse sequence, different contrasts may be generated between tissues based on the relaxation properties of the hydrogen atoms therein.
Since its development in the 1970s and 1980s, MRI has proven to be a versatile imaging technique. While MRI is most prominently used in diagnostic medicine and biomedical research, it also may be used to form images of non-living objects, such as mummies. Diffusion MRI and functional MRI extend the utility of MRI to capture neuronal tracts and blood flow respectively in the nervous system, in addition to detailed spatial images. The sustained increase in demand for MRI within health systems has led to concerns about cost effectiveness and overdiagnosis.[dubious  – discuss]

So that 's port and starboard for you : the loading side and the steering side .   Bow   is an old word that originally meant an animal 's shoulders , so where the sides of the ship curved at the front was considered to be the ship 's   shoulders   . It 's not clear where   stern   comes from , but it may be again related to steering , since the steering rudder was not only on the right side of the ship , but also at the back . But that 's conjecture -- nobody seems to know for sure . Why do n't they use the normal English words ? Well ... why should they ? Gears control how much force your car can send to the wheels . If you want to accelerate rapidly , you want to be in a lower gear . The downside to low gears is that the engine spins very fast , and so you soon ca n't make the engine go any faster ( like cycling on a bike in a low gear when your legs go round as fast as they can , yet you do n't go very fast . ) In order to go at higher speeds , you need to shift into a higher gear . This means the engine can go at a lower speed ( RPM ) while the car goes at the same speed . Then accelerating speeds the engine back up , which thanks to the higher gear , results in a faster speed for the car . Lower gears are better for accelerating , Higher gears are better for having a higher top - speed . Higher gears are also more fuel efficient , since your engine wastes energy the faster it goes . If you are starting from stationary , you want to be in 1st gear , then as you accelerate to ~10 mph you will hear your engine start to whine as the RPM gets high , you should now change up to 2nd gear . Conversely if you are doing 70 mph on a motorway in 5th gear and slow down to 40pmh make a turning you are now in too high a gear for your speed , and the engine will struggle to accelerate . You should change down to 4th gear as you brake , so your car is ready to accelerate away afterwards . When going down a steep hill , you want to change down to a lower gear to keep your car from getting too fast . When going up hill , you also want a lower gear to provide more force to overcome gravity . Lower gear - > more resistance , more acceleration Higher gear - > less resistance , less acceleration

A computer network is a set of computers sharing resources located on or provided by network nodes. The computers use common communication protocols over digital interconnections to communicate with each other. These interconnections are made up of telecommunication network technologies, based on physically wired, optical, and wireless radio-frequency methods that may be arranged in a variety of network topologies.
The nodes of a computer network can include personal computers, servers, networking hardware, or other specialised or general-purpose hosts. They are identified by network addresses, and may have hostnames. Hostnames serve as memorable labels for the nodes, rarely changed after initial assignment. Network addresses serve for locating and identifying the nodes by communication protocols such as the Internet Protocol.
Computer networks may be classified by many criteria, including the transmission medium used to carry signals, bandwidth, communications protocols to organize network traffic, the network size, the topology, traffic control mechanism, and organizational intent.
Computer networks support many applications and services, such as access to the World Wide Web, digital video, digital audio, shared use of application and storage servers, printers, and fax machines, and use of email and instant messaging applications.

well , a transistor is like a light switch controlled by another light switch . seems kinda simple and pointless , but when you connect a ton of them together in specific patterns they can do interesting things . Species - A species is a group of organisms capable of interbreeding and producing fertile offspring . Domestic dogs are a single species ( Canis lupus familiaris ) . Domestic cats are a single species ( Felis silvestris catus ) . Modern humans are a single species ( homo sapiens sapiens ) . The difference between a pit bull terrier , a poodle and a basset hound are superficial , these are identified as   breeds .   The same is true of house cats ( Siamese , Maine Coon , Persian , etc ) . These superficial differences are similar to the differences between humans that are from different   races   ( Caucasian , Eastern Asian , African , etc ) . The more pronounced differences seen in domesticated animals are a product of more selective breeding and a greater number of generations that have been subject to said breeding . If you want to talk about different species of dogs , cats and humans , you have to look at the next order up , which in the   genus .   For each you have : Cats : Felis ( wildcat , sand cat , jungle cat , domestic cat ) . Dog : Canis ( Jackal , Coyote , Wolves / domestic dog ) Human : Homo These are different species that look very similar , but since they are distinct species , they can not interbreed with a fertile offspring . You 'll note that   wolf   and   domestic dog   is actually the same species . So , why are there no listings for the   homo   family ? Because they are extinct . The only one that has a easily recognizable name is the Homo neanderthalensis ( Neandarthal ) . There are , however , several others : > Homo gautengensis > Homo habilis > Homo erectus > Homo antecessor > Homo ergaster > Homo rhodesiensis > Homo heidelbergensis > Homo floresiensis Some of these are direct fore - bearers of modern humans , others are different evolutionary branches that just did n't survive ( there are examples of this among cats and dogs , too but I did n't feel the need to go into that ) .

All numbers inside a computer are stored in binary - which means they are made up of 1s and 0s . Each digit in binary is called a   bit   . So the number of bits indicated the number of digits it can work with . In decimal , a 2 - digit number can be a number between 0 - 99 , and a 4 - digit number can be a number between 0 - 9999 . Well , it 's the same in binary . The more bits , the higher the numbers you can work with . What difference does this make ? Well , each byte in memory has an   address   which is a number , so the more digits ( bits ) you use , the more addresses you can handle , and so the more memory you can handle . It also affects how numbers are handled internally . It can take longer to do certain operations involving big numbers ( you might not even realise that the computer is using big numbers ) if the computer ca n't represent them directly . Some computers can handle only 32 - bit software , because either the processor or the operating system only knows how to run in 32 - bit mode . Other computers can handle 32 - bit or 64 - bit software . It 's usually a good idea to run 64 - bit software when you can , but for everyday use it probably makes very little difference .

In the United States, the world of stock trading operates a little differently than you might expect if you're new to investing. While stocks are typically listed on a single exchange—such as the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) or the Nasdaq—that doesn’t mean they’re confined to that one marketplace. Instead, once a stock is officially listed, it can actually be traded across various venues beyond its original exchange. This gives investors more flexibility and options for buying or selling shares, while also creating competition among trading platforms.

To break it down further, think of an exchange like the Nasdaq or NYSE as a home base for a stock. When a company goes public, its shares are listed on one of these major exchanges, which act as the primary location where information about the stock—like its price, performance history, and market cap—is centralized. But in today’s fast-paced financial landscape, stock trades can occur in many other places, including alternative trading systems (ATS) and electronic communication networks (ECNs). These platforms allow institutional investors or even smaller traders to move shares outside of traditional exchanges. The end result? A more fragmented but flexible ecosystem that accommodates different types of traders and investment strategies.

This setup has been largely driven by technological advancements that make it easier to trade electronically. At first glance, it might seem chaotic to have trades happening across so many venues. However, this system ultimately fosters liquidity and ensures competitive pricing. In practice, it means you don’t necessarily have to limit your transactions to the exchange where a stock is listed—you might find a better deal elsewhere. For many investors, this openness enhances access and opportunity in an increasingly digital financial world.

So, let's talk about leases, which are basically just a way to rent something, like a car, for a specific period. When you lease, you're essentially borrowing money to cover the expected decrease in value—the depreciation—of that car during the time you'll be using it.

Imagine you decide to lease a new car instead of buying it outright. You're not paying for the entire value of the car; instead, you're covering the part that the car is likely to lose in value by the time your lease is up. This usually results in lower monthly payments compared to purchasing because you're financing only a portion of the vehicle's worth.

Think of leasing as agreeing to use a car until it starts losing its "newness." When your lease ends, the car will have depreciated, meaning it's not worth as much as when you first got it. You've been paying for this predicted drop in value over time.

There’s an upside and downside to this arrangement. On one hand, leasing might offer advantages like lower monthly payments and possibly driving a newer car every few years without worrying about selling your old one or dealing with trade-ins. Plus, leases often include maintenance perks since you're supposed to keep the car in good condition. 

On the flip side, leasing means you don't actually own the car. You'll face mileage limits and potential penalties if you drive more than agreed upon or damage it beyond normal wear and tear. So if you're someone who prefers long road trips or wants to modify your ride freely, leasing might not be ideal for you.

Ultimately, leasing can be a great option if your goal is affordability and convenience rather than ownership and flexibility.

Satellites orbit Earth at altitudes that vary greatly depending on their purpose and function. While it might be tempting to imagine these paths as immense circles or spheres enveloping the planet, the truth is more nuanced. Satellite orbits can range from relatively close to the surface, in low Earth orbit, up to thousands of miles away in geostationary orbit. These paths are not strictly spherical; rather, they form ellipses or circular trajectories influenced by gravitational forces and mission objectives.

For instance, low Earth orbit satellites travel just a few hundred miles above the surface. In contrast, geostationary satellites orbit at an astonishing 22,236 miles above Earth. Each of these orbits serves different roles—low Earth orbit for imagery and communications with reduced latency and geostationary for broader coverage and stable communications networks.

Despite variations in altitude and shape, these orbital paths are indeed vast when compared to Earth's diameter of about 7,917 miles. However, describing them as "spheres significantly larger than the entire Earth" might oversimplify their complexity. It's essential to appreciate the diverse functions and precise calculations involved in positioning these technological marvels as they encircle our planet at varying distances.

Ultimately, selecting the right model involves understanding the specific needs of an organization or application, as well as considering factors like scalability and ease of maintenance.

With technological advancements continuously reshaping data requirements, the importance of choosing an appropriate database model cannot be overstated. A well-chosen model can lead to more streamlined operations and enhanced decision-making capabilities by ensuring that data is both accessible and actionable when needed.

Alright, let’s break this down in a way that’s easier to understand. Classification, when it comes to stats, is basically about sorting things into categories. Imagine you have a bunch of data, and you’re trying to figure out which group each piece of data belongs to—kind of like organizing socks by color or size.

For example, let’s say you’re working with information about animals. You could use classification to decide whether each animal in your dataset is a cat, dog, or bird based on certain features—maybe fur type, weight, or whether it can fly. The goal is to match each observation (in this case, an individual animal) to the right category (like cat, dog, or bird).

This process isn’t limited to animals though; it works for all kinds of stuff. You might be looking at customer data and trying to predict whether someone is likely to buy your product based on their age or shopping habits. Or maybe you’re analyzing medical test results and determining whether a patient falls into the “healthy” group or the “needs follow-up” group.

Basically, classification is all about using patterns in your data to make decisions about where something fits. And with the help of tools like machine learning algorithms (fancy programs that learn from examples), you can get pretty good at sorting things quickly and accurately—even with complex datasets.

So yeah, at its core, classification is just about taking something you don’t know much about yet and figuring out where it belongs based on the data you have. It’s super useful in everything from science to business!

Old English and modern English are not considered the same language, which is why we refer to it as "Old English." This ancient form of the language, spoken and written from around the 5th to the 11th century, differs significantly from the English we use today. It evolved over centuries, influenced by various cultural and linguistic changes, including the Norman Conquest, which introduced many French elements into the language.

Old English had a rich vocabulary and a unique grammatical structure, featuring different sounds and letters that might seem unfamiliar to us now. It can be difficult for a modern English speaker to understand Old English without specific study. Some of its most famous texts include "Beowulf" and "The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle," which offer glimpses into life during that period. These works highlight the language’s complexity and beauty, showing how it served as a foundation for the evolution of modern English.

Understanding Old English allows us to appreciate how languages transform over time and provides insight into our linguistic heritage. Although it is no longer spoken in its original form, Old English remains an important part of the historical tapestry of our language.

Digital signatures are a fascinating application of public key cryptography, a concept that plays a crucial role in securing online communication and ensuring authenticity. To understand the basics, it can help to start with simpler encryption methods, like the classic rotation cipher. You may already be familiar with this technique—it’s essentially what many people think of when they imagine secret codes. A rotation cipher works by shifting letters in the alphabet by a fixed number of places. For instance, if you were using a rotation of three, “A” would become “D,” “B” would become “E,” and so on.

While fun and easy to understand, a rotation cipher is fairly straightforward to crack, which makes it impractical for modern cybersecurity needs. This is where public key cryptography steps in. It’s an advanced form of encryption that relies on pairs of keys: one public and one private. The public key is widely shared and used for encrypting messages or verifying digital signatures, while the private key is kept secret and is used for decrypting information or creating signatures.

So why does this matter? Digital signatures are like handwritten signatures but far more secure. They allow individuals or organizations to prove that a document hasn’t been tampered with and confirm the identity of the sender. For instance, when you sign an email or authorize a transaction online using your private key, the recipient can verify its legitimacy using your public key.

By combining cryptographic principles with practical applications, digital signatures have become an essential tool for everything from e-commerce to government communications. They ensure trust in the digital age—an era where protecting sensitive data is more important than ever. Although rooted in complex mathematics, their role ultimately boils down to something simple: keeping our online interactions safe and reliable.

A paradox is a fascinating linguistic and philosophical construct that challenges our understanding of logic and reality. To illustrate, consider the classic example known as the "liar paradox," which is encapsulated in the statement, "This sentence is false." At first glance, the sentence appears straightforward, but upon closer inspection, it raises a conundrum: if the sentence is true, then it must be false as it claims; however, if it is false, then it must be true because it's correctly stating its falsity. This cyclical loop defies conventional logic and leaves us questioning the boundaries of language and truth. Paradoxes play crucial roles beyond intellectual exercises; they often serve as catalysts for breakthroughs in thought. In mathematics, Zeno’s paradoxes famously challenged notions of motion and infinity, prompting advancements in calculus and continuous functions to resolve them. In physics, quantum mechanics deals with phenomena that seem paradoxical to classical interpretations of reality. Moreover, paradoxes are not confined to abstract realms; they permeate everyday life and decision-making. Consider scenarios like the "paradox of choice," where more options lead to less satisfaction due to overwhelming decision-making pressures. Here, a seemingly reasonable premise—more choices equal better outcomes—results in the contrary. In literature and art, paradoxes enrich narratives and imagery with layers of meaning and complexity. They compel audiences to engage with content on deeper levels, encouraging them to question appearances and consider multiple perspectives. Thus, while a paradox may initially appear as an impossibility born from conflicting truths, it serves as a valuable tool for expanding our understanding. When it comes to purchasing something significant—whether it's a car, a property, or another big-ticket item—you’re often faced with several financing options, each with its own advantages and drawbacks. The decision ultimately depends on your financial situation, your long-term goals, and how comfortable you are with taking on debt.

One option is to buy outright and pay in full. While this approach eliminates the burden of loans or monthly repayments, it also depletes your savings entirely. If you’re in a strong financial position and can comfortably afford to pay upfront without jeopardizing your emergency fund or future plans, this can be a smart move. However, for many people, the idea of draining their savings is a risk they’d rather not take.

The second option is to split the cost—putting down a substantial deposit (say, £10,000) while financing the remainder through a loan (£4,000). This middle ground reduces the immediate financial strain but also means you’ll still have some debt to manage. Depending on interest rates and loan terms, this can offer flexibility without entirely wiping out your savings.

Alternatively, you could explore financing arrangements like Personal Contract Purchase (PCP) or Hire Purchase (HP). These methods allow you to spread payments over time for larger portions of the item's value. While they often come with interest costs and sometimes restrictive conditions, they might be more appealing if preserving cash flow is your priority.

Ultimately, weighing these choices requires a clear understanding of your finances today—and what sacrifices you’re willing to make for the future.

At its core, the active contour model is designed to evolve over time. It cleverly balances internal forces, which smooth and regularize the contour, with external forces that attract it toward desired features in the image, such as edges or boundaries.

The ingenuity of this approach lies in its ability to adapt dynamically to different scenarios and achieve a level of precision that static methods might miss. Instead of relying solely on predefined shapes or rigid models, snakes can flex and change shape as they zero in on their target. This flexibility is especially crucial in fields like medical imaging or satellite imagery analysis, where clarity and detail are paramount.

As technology has advanced, so too have applications for active contour models. From segmenting anatomical structures in MRI scans to identifying objects within aerial photographs, these dynamic contours continue to play a critical role. By effectively tackling noise and distortion within images, they enable more accurate interpretations and decisions based on visual data—a true testament to their lasting impact in the world of computer vision.

In Brazil, the electoral system is quite different from those in countries like the United States, where district-based voting is common. Here, we use a system of proportional representation in which votes are cast for parties rather than individual candidates. This might lead to some confusion when trying to understand the concept of district voting or gerrymandering as it occurs elsewhere. Allow me to explain as best as I can from an outside perspective.

District voting refers to an electoral system in which a country or region is divided into districts, with each district electing its own representative. In systems like these, voters within a specific geographic area select their representative to a larger legislative body. This can lead to discrepancies and manipulation—a term known as gerrymandering—where district boundaries are drawn in ways that favor one party or group over another.

For example, imagine a country divided into several districts. If one political party controls the process of drawing these boundaries, they might adjust them in such a way that maximizes their chances of winning more seats. This can be achieved by clustering opposition voters into fewer districts, thus allowing the ruling party to win more districts with fewer votes—a process known as "packing and cracking."

In contrast, Brazil's system is designed to allocate seats proportionally based on the total number of votes each party receives across a larger region or even nationwide. This aims to ensure that representation in legislative bodies more closely reflects the political makeup of the population at large.

While both systems have their pros and cons, understanding these differences highlights how varying electoral frameworks can influence political outcomes and voter representation. The absence of district voting in Brazil prevents gerrymandering, but it also creates its own set of challenges and dynamics within our political landscape.

This provision generally applies if your ownership exceeds 5% of a company’s outstanding shares. 

Once you cross this threshold, you’re required to file a Schedule 13D with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). This filing serves as an official notice to the market and provides detailed information about your ownership stake, intentions regarding the investment, and any plans that could potentially impact the company’s governance or operations. The disclosure helps ensure transparency in cases where significant stakeholders could exert substantial influence over corporate affairs.

It’s worth noting that these requirements are especially pertinent in the context of U.S.-based stocks. Similar regulations exist in other jurisdictions but may vary in scope or application. Ultimately, Section 13(d) exists to maintain fairness in financial markets by providing both investors and companies with insight into material ownership changes that could alter the balance of power within a firm.

The phrase "post hoc, ergo propter hoc" comes from Latin and translates to "after this, therefore because of this." It's often used to describe a logical fallacy where someone assumes that just because one event follows another, the first must have caused the second. While it’s tempting to draw connections between sequential events, correlation doesn’t always equal causation. For example, imagine you wake up with a headache on the same day your neighbor paints their fence. It might be tempting to blame the fumes for your discomfort simply because the painting happened first. However, without evidence linking the two, it’s just an assumption—a classic post hoc fallacy.  

This kind of reasoning can sneak into everyday life more easily than we realize. It’s human nature to look for patterns or explanations for the things we experience. But jumping to conclusions without considering other possible factors can lead us astray. Understanding this fallacy is not just useful in logic or debate; it can help us become more thoughtful in analyzing cause-and-effect relationships in all areas of life—from personal decisions to broader societal trends. Taking a moment to ask "Is this really connected, or am I just assuming?" can make all the difference in arriving at clearer insights.

Rain is one of those natural phenomena that seems simple at first glance but is actually the result of complex interactions within our atmosphere. At its core, rain requires two fundamental components: moist air and a mechanism to release that moisture from the sky. Moist air is laden with water vapor, which is an essential ingredient for precipitation. This vapor originates from bodies of water like oceans, lakes, and rivers, as well as from plant transpiration and evaporation. When the air is saturated with this vapor, it becomes primed for rain.

However, having moist air alone isn't enough; there must be a catalyst to trigger the rainfall. This catalyst usually comes in the form of atmospheric conditions that cool the air and cause it to condense. It can be a weather front where different temperatures collide or changes in air pressure that elevate moist air higher into the atmosphere where it cools rapidly. When cooled sufficiently, the water vapor condenses into droplets that coalesce into clouds. Eventually, these droplets become heavy enough to fall as rain.

In essence, rain is a beautifully orchestrated dance between moisture and atmospheric dynamics—nature's way of ensuring life on Earth continues to thrive amidst an ever-changing sky.

In the early days of sailing, ships were designed with two primary sides known as larboard and starboard. These terms, deeply rooted in nautical tradition, referred to the left and right sides of a vessel when facing forward towards the bow. The starboard side, derived from the Old English "steorbord," signified the side on which the steering oar or rudder was mounted—typically the right side of the ship. This was because most sailors were right-handed, making it more practical to steer from this position.

On the other hand, the term larboard originated from "ladebord," which referred to the loading side of a ship. This was generally the port, or left side, where cargo and supplies were loaded and unloaded. Over time, however, it became apparent that having two similar-sounding terms—larboard and starboard—could lead to confusion during critical navigation moments or in rough weather conditions. Imagine a bustling deck where shouted commands needed to be understood instantly; such ambiguity could prove disastrous.

To resolve this potential hazard, "port" was officially adopted in place of "larboard" in the mid-19th century. The term "port" not only eliminated confusion but also offered a fitting reminder that this side of the ship typically faced the dock when loading.

Thus, modern ships now refer to their sides as port and starboard—a testament to centuries-old maritime practices that prioritize clarity and safety for sailors navigating through vast and unpredictable seas. These terms have become so integral that they transcend nautical use, symbolizing precision and legacy in language worldwide.

When we think about air and how it behaves, temperature plays a significant role in determining its properties—density being one of them. Hot air, for example, has a lower density compared to air at room temperature. This happens because heating the air causes the molecules within it to move more rapidly and spread further apart. As a result, the same volume of hot air contains fewer molecules than cooler, denser air. 

You can observe this phenomenon in everyday life. For instance, when you heat up a balloon or watch a hot air balloon rise into the sky, you're witnessing this principle in action. The heated air inside the balloon becomes less dense than the cooler surrounding air, allowing the balloon to float upward. When the air around us is already heavy with moisture—what we often refer to as high humidity—it becomes harder for sweat to evaporate. As a result, instead of evaporating and carrying heat away from our bodies, sweat tends to sit on our skin, making us feel sticky and uncomfortably hot.

On drier days, when the air isn’t saturated with water, sweat evaporates more easily. This helps regulate our body temperature more effectively, leaving us feeling cooler even in warm weather. It’s why humid summer days often feel so much worse than dry ones with the same temperature. Understanding this relationship between sweating and air saturation is key to knowing why some environments feel unbearable—and why staying hydrated matters so much when we’re trying to keep cool!

Communism and capitalism are two fundamentally distinct economic systems, yet they share the commonality of being frameworks designed to manage resources, production, and distribution within a society. In a communist system, the means of production—such as factories, land, and resources—are owned collectively or by the state rather than by private individuals. The goal is to achieve equality by ensuring that wealth and goods are distributed according to people’s needs rather than based on market forces or profit motives. Communism aspires to create a society where individuals contribute based on their abilities and receive based on their needs, reducing disparities in wealth and power.

Capitalism, on the other hand, emphasizes private ownership of property and businesses. It is driven by market dynamics, competition, and individual enterprise. Wealth is generated through profit-making ventures, with prices determined by supply and demand in free markets. In capitalist economies, inequality is often seen as an inevitable byproduct because rewards are tied to productivity, innovation, and investment.

Though both systems serve as economic models for organizing society, their approaches reflect contrasting philosophies about human nature, resource allocation, and social priorities.

Instead, they become part of the institution's pool of resources.

Banks operate by using deposits to fund loans and invest in various financial instruments. This is a cornerstone of how modern banking works—they take the money entrusted by depositors and use it for lending and investing purposes while ensuring there’s sufficient liquidity to meet withdrawal demands. The money you see in your account is essentially an IOU from the bank, backed by their obligation to honor your request when you withdraw or transfer funds.

This distinction highlights why banks are considered intermediaries rather than mere safekeepers. While they offer convenience, security, and services like interest-bearing accounts or loans, they don’t function as vaults where your cash remains unaltered and untouched. Understanding this principle can give deeper insight into how banks operate and why trust in financial institutions—and regulatory frameworks—plays such a critical role. Inside a computer, all numbers are stored in binary — a system made up entirely of 1s and 0s. This might sound like something out of science fiction, but it’s the foundation of how computers process and understand information. Each individual digit in this binary system is called a “bit,” short for “binary digit.” While it may seem strange at first to think of numbers being stored in such a simplified way, the binary system is actually incredibly efficient for machines.

In essence, each bit represents either an “on” or “off” state, similar to flipping a light switch. By combining bits together into larger groupings, computers can represent more complex values. For example, eight bits grouped together form a "byte," which can represent anything from a single character in text to part of an image or sound. With enough combinations, computers can perform advanced calculations, store massive amounts of data, and execute instructions with astonishing speed.

Binary might feel counterintuitive to humans since we’re used to the decimal system — counting with digits from 0 through 9 — but for machines built on circuits and logic gates, binary is much simpler to work with. It's the backbone of everything a computer does: from basic math operations to running sophisticated software applications.

So while we rarely interact with binary directly in our daily lives, it’s working behind the scenes every time we send a text message, stream a movie, or scroll through social media. It’s amazing to think that so much complexity boils down to an elegant series of 1s and 0s — proof that sometimes simplicity really is the key to unlocking incredible possibilities!
